title: Repeated DCOM Registration or Remote-Activation Failures
exclusions: This use case reports repeated Microsoft-Windows-DistributedCOM System-channel Event 10010 or 10028 groups. Event 10010 says that the named COM server did not register with DCOM within the required timeout; Event 10028 says that a requesting process could not communicate with a named remote computer using configured protocols during activation. It does not prove an application outage, broken registration, permissions fault, malicious activity, RPC-port block, DNS fault, process crash, or specific root cause. It does not monitor all COM/DCOM/COM+ errors, COM+ application state, local/remote activation success, RPC latency, service health, or application transactions. Event 10016 is intentionally excluded: Microsoft documents common built-in 10016 events as expected, by-design, and safe to ignore, and warns that permission changes can have unintended effects. A five-minute collection delay and three-event threshold can miss isolated or late failures. Event templates can vary by Windows build; deploy only after local XML validation.
evidence: After deployment, retain the Windows host/application/DCOM dependency and owner inventory; supported Windows builds and expected remote targets/components; locally exported Event 10010 and 10028 XML templates with provider, channel, version, message, and `param1`-`param4` mapping; approved baseline and threshold rationale; effective `[WinEventLog://System]` XML input, `Splunk_TA_windows` version, deployment-server state, `btool` output, source type/index, collection lag, and telemetry-health results; the `windows_repeated_dcom_activation_failure` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and triggered alerts; each result's UTC bounds, host, event type, component/target/requester context, record IDs, message hashes, and raw-event references; correlated application/service/process-crash, SCM, DNS, RPC endpoint/firewall, network, patch/change, reboot, and remote-host evidence; bounded exception approvals; incident disposition and recovery; and dated positive, negative, threshold, template-variation, maintenance, stale-source, and end-to-end tests. This documentation-only review changed no DCOM, COM+, registry, service, firewall, RPC, application, or Splunk production configuration and generated no event or alert evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest three XML-shaped System events in the closed window with provider `Microsoft-Windows-DistributedCOM`, EventCode 10010, the same `dest`, and `param1={11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111}`; expect one `dcom_server_registration_timeout` row with `failure_events=3`. Separately ingest three Event 10028 records for one host with `param1=legacy-mgmt01.example.test`, `param2=1a2b`, `param3=C:\Windows\System32\ServerManager.exe`, and `param4={22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222}`; expect one `dcom_remote_activation_communication_failure` row preserving target, requester, CLSID, three record IDs, and three message hashes.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for two matching 10010 events; two matching 10028 events; any number of Event 10016 records; Event 10010 from another provider/channel; Event 10010 without `param1`; Event 10028 without remote target or requester process; otherwise valid events in the newest excluded five minutes; and three events split across different hosts, server identifiers, remote targets, requester paths, or activation CLSIDs. Verify a later healthy application transaction does not erase historical base results but closes the incident through separate recovery logic.

dataSources: Windows System event log collected locally in XML from expected Windows clients and servers. The exact contract is `source=XmlWinEventLog:System`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, provider `Microsoft-Windows-DistributedCOM`, and Event IDs 10010 and 10028. Required common fields are `_time`, `dest`/`Computer`, `EventCode`/`EventID`, provider, `EventRecordID`, `Message`, `source`, and `sourcetype`. For Event 10010, locally validate `param1` as the server identifier from the message. For Event 10028, locally validate `param1` as remote computer, `param2` as requester PID, `param3` as requester executable, and `param4` as activation CLSID when the installed event template emits it. XML/template exports are authoritative for each supported build; do not infer missing parameters from position or message language.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1 for Windows event-log collection and field normalization, plus a local `windows_dcom_monitor` app containing the reviewed XML input, saved search, lookup-based routing/exceptions, source-health search, and dashboard.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:System" EventCode IN (10010,10028) earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), dest=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,Computer,host))), provider=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName,SourceName), record_id=tostring(coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber,"not_extracted"))
| where provider="Microsoft-Windows-DistributedCOM" AND len(dest)>0 AND (event_code=10010 OR event_code=10028)
| eval component_id=if(event_code=10010,coalesce(trim(param1),"not_extracted"),coalesce(trim(param4),"not_provided")), remote_target=if(event_code=10028,lower(coalesce(trim(param1),"not_extracted")),"not_applicable"), requester_pid=if(event_code=10028,lower(coalesce(trim(param2),"not_extracted")),"not_applicable"), requester_process=if(event_code=10028,lower(coalesce(trim(param3),"not_extracted")),"not_applicable")
| where (event_code=10010 AND component_id!="not_extracted") OR (event_code=10028 AND remote_target!="not_extracted" AND requester_process!="not_extracted")
| eval issue=if(event_code=10010,"dcom_server_registration_timeout","dcom_remote_activation_communication_failure"), message_hash=sha256(coalesce(Message,_raw)), use_case="UC-1.2.59"
| stats earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen count as failure_events values(requester_pid) as requester_pids values(record_id) as record_ids values(message_hash) as message_hashes by dest event_code issue component_id remote_target requester_process source sourcetype use_case
| where failure_events>=3
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| table first_seen last_seen dest issue event_code component_id remote_target requester_process requester_pids failure_events record_ids message_hashes source sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 -failure_events dest issue component_id remote_target
description: Reports a host/component or host/remote-target/requester group when at least three DistributedCOM registration timeouts (10010) or remote-activation communication failures (10028) occur in a closed 15-minute window. It excludes noisy 10016 permission events and preserves event-specific identifiers needed to connect the symptom to an owned application or remote dependency.
value: A recurring COM-server registration timeout can delay or break a dependent application, while repeated remote DCOM activation failures can expose an unreachable host, stale dependency, or RPC path problem. Grouping only identical failure contexts reduces diagnostic time by turning opaque System-log messages into actionable component and dependency evidence without treating every DCOM event as an outage.
implementation: Collect the local System channel as XML on inventoried Windows hosts, validate the installed 10010/10028 event templates on each supported build, and maintain component/remote-target ownership. Save the SPL as `windows_repeated_dcom_activation_failure`; schedule every 5 minutes over the delayed 15-minute window; trigger per result grain; and correlate with application impact before paging. Keep Event 10016 outside this rule. Test both branches, threshold boundaries, event-field absence, reboot/patch/maintenance patterns, stale targets, source health, and safe recovery. Never automate DCOM ACL, registry, service, firewall, or component-registration changes from this alert.
visualization: Build a DCOM dependency dashboard with System-log freshness and XML-field completeness first; single values for active 10010 groups, active 10028 groups, affected hosts, and remote targets; a stacked timechart by issue; tables for 10010 server identifiers and 10028 target/requester/CLSID pairs; and a host-to-target dependency view. Drill down to raw XML/message, owning application/service, process and crash events, SCM state, DNS resolution, RPC endpoint/firewall/network telemetry, target availability, recent reboot/patch/change, and incident recovery. Label counts as repeated DCOM symptoms, not confirmed outages or security incidents.
schema: Native Microsoft-Windows-DistributedCOM System-channel XML Events 10010 and 10028
dataModelAcceleration: No CIM data model is claimed. CIM Change and Application State do not preserve these native DCOM event semantics, event-template parameters, server identifier, remote target, requester process/PID, activation CLSID, or source-health context. If scale requires summary acceleration, retain one row per event and all alert-grain fields, record/message evidence, source metadata, event-template version, and lateness markers; prove summary-to-raw parity before alerting.

knownFalsePositives:
A matching event group is a true repeated DCOM symptom under the stated event contract, but it may be expected or non-impacting. Distinguish operational context before paging.

1. **Boot, sign-in, or shutdown timing** — Packaged apps, brokers, services, or user components can miss registration timing during startup or teardown without persistent impact. Correlate boot/session boundaries, service state, later successful application transaction, recurrence outside the boundary, and exact server identifier.

2. **Patch or application deployment restart** — A replaced executable/service can produce 10010 while stopping, registering, or starting. Verify package/build, signed change, owner, exact host/component, service/process timeline, successful smoke test, and bounded UTC window.

3. **Approved remote-host maintenance** — Event 10028 is expected if a requester activates a component while the target is rebooting, isolated, or drained. Match exact source host, target, requester, change, maintenance bounds, and later RPC/application recovery; do not suppress unrelated targets or post-window failures.

4. **Stale inventory, Server Manager entry, scheduled task, or application endpoint** — Repeated activation of a decommissioned/renamed target is a real configuration defect rather than a live-target outage. Confirm DNS/IP, CMDB retirement, requester configuration/task, target owner, and remove the stale dependency through change control.

5. **Optional feature or best-effort discovery** — An application can attempt DCOM and then succeed through another path. Prove the fallback with application logs/transaction outcome and owner documentation; suppress only the exact requester-target-component tuple, not all 10028 events.

6. **Slow or resource-constrained COM server startup** — CPU, disk, profile, dependency, or service delay can cause 10010 and then recover. Correlate process/service start, performance, crash/hang, dependency and transaction evidence. Repeated latency remains actionable even when eventual registration succeeds.

7. **Expected lab or resilience test** — A controlled target isolation, firewall, service-stop, or registration-timeout test should create the relevant branch. Match test ID, exact entities, operator, safety controls, expected count/time, alert delivery, restoration, and successful recovery; retain as control evidence.

8. **Duplicate event collection** — Two WinEventLog inputs/forwarders can inflate a two-event symptom over threshold. Compare `EventRecordID`, source/host/forwarder metadata, input deployment, and hashes; correct collection and keep deduplication observable.

**Safe suppression:** preserve raw events and base-search results. Apply notification exceptions after detection through a reviewed lookup keyed to exact host, event code, server identifier or remote target, requester path, optional CLSID, owner, reason/change/test ID, and exclusive epoch bounds. Reject provider-wide, EventCode-wide, host-wide permanent, wildcard-target, or blanket maintenance exclusions. Never suppress missing/stale System-log collection, unexpected target/component drift, worsening frequency, correlated application failure, remote-target unavailability, process crash, or absent recovery.
hardware: Supported Windows clients and servers that run or request owned COM/DCOM components. Remote DCOM dependencies require source/target ownership, DNS and RPC-path context; the event is logged on the requesting/observing host and is not a target-side health assertion.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Microsoft COM registration, DCOM/RPC connectivity and port guidance, Microsoft's explicit Event 10016 recommendation, locally verifiable Event 10010/10028 XML examples, and Splunk Windows XML event-log/add-on documentation; Windows-build templates, field extraction, baselines, dependencies, fixtures, impact, alert delivery, exceptions, remediation, and recovery were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Windows/application/network/Splunk SME-signed

cost.search_load_notes: The search scans only two event IDs from one System channel over a delayed 15-minute window and aggregates low-cardinality failure contexts. Retain source-health and duplicate-input checks because missing or duplicated System logs can hide or inflate the threshold.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and semantic boundary

Assign owners for each Windows host, application/service, COM server identifier, remote DCOM dependency, DNS/network/firewall/RPC path, Windows platform, Splunk collection/content, telemetry health, and incident response. Inventory expected source hosts and builds, application/service and user/session context, known Event 10010 identifiers, Event 10028 requester executable/target/optional CLSID tuples, critical transaction, maintenance pattern, and escalation path. A GUID-like string is not sufficient ownership: resolve it through approved application inventory and locally read-only registration evidence, then have the application owner confirm it.

This UC deliberately narrows the old “DCOM / COM+ errors” claim. Microsoft describes COM objects as in-process, local out-of-process, or remote; COM registration tells Windows where and how a CLSID's server code is launched. Event 10010 records only that the named server did not register with DCOM within the required timeout. The identifier may be a GUID or a runtime/application class string. It does not itself say “registration is corrupt,” “permission denied,” or “process crashed.” Event 10028 records that DCOM could not communicate with the named remote computer using configured protocols for a request; supported templates can also carry requester PID/path and activation CLSID. It does not prove which network, DNS, firewall, endpoint, authentication, service, or application condition caused the failure.

Event 10016 is excluded. Microsoft's current support article says the listed built-in 10016 access attempts are expected and by design, safely ignored, and that changing component permissions can have unintended side effects. Do not convert generic 10016 volume into a fault alert or automate ACL edits. This UC also makes no COM+ catalog/application-state or security-detection claim.

## Step 1 — Validate templates and collect XML

On a canary for every supported Windows build/application pattern, export representative 10010 and 10028 events from Event Viewer or `Get-WinEvent` with XML. Record Provider Name, provider GUID, channel, EventID, Version, rendered message, Correlation/Execution values, and every named EventData element. Verify 10010 `param1` exactly matches the server identifier in the rendered message. Verify 10028 `param1` remote computer, `param2` requester PID, `param3` requester path, and whether that template emits `param4` activation CLSID. Do not assume a missing `param4`, localized message, or different event version has the same layout; version the field contract and add canary fixtures.

Use the Universal Forwarder and reviewed local app rather than remote polling. Example local input:

```ini
[WinEventLog://System]
disabled = 0
renderXml = 1
index = wineventlog
```

Merge with the organization's existing System input—never deploy a duplicate stanza merely for this UC. Splunk documents `renderXml=1`; if input-side XML filtering is used, follow the documented `$XmlRegex` behavior and prove 10010/10028 plus source-health events are retained. Keep `source=XmlWinEventLog:System` and `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` aligned with the deployed TA behavior. Inspect `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, deployment-app precedence, forwarder identity, permissions, index routing, and lag. Validate `Provider_Name`, `EventCode`, `Computer`/`dest`, `EventRecordID`, `Message`, and named parameters in indexed raw XML.

Build companion telemetry checks for expected host with no recent System events, missing provider/event extraction, unknown event version, null required parameters, duplicate EventRecordID, future/late timestamps, host identity drift, TA/input version drift, and duplicate collectors. Silence is unknown, not “no DCOM failures.” Preserve raw XML under the approved retention/access policy; event messages can expose internal hostnames and executable paths.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the threshold search

Save the SPL as `windows_repeated_dcom_activation_failure` and schedule every 5 minutes. At 12:20, `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m` evaluates 12:00–12:15 and leaves five minutes for forwarding. Measure p95/p99 lag and move both bounds together if needed. Trigger one result per full aggregation grain and throttle duplicate notification briefly while retaining each base result. The threshold of three identical-context events is an explicit starter policy, not a Microsoft default; backtest 30 days by host/application and obtain owner approval.

The first stage uses exact index/source/sourcetype/EventCode predicates. `eval` normalizes event ID, host, provider, and record identity; `where` rejects provider/channel collisions. For 10010, `component_id` comes from validated `param1`; remote/requester dimensions become `not_applicable`. For 10028, remote target, requester PID/path, and optional CLSID are mapped from validated named elements. Required context is fail-closed: a 10010 without server identifier and a 10028 without target or requester path cannot alert and must be caught by field-health logic.

`message_hash` supports evidence comparison without placing the full message in the result. `stats` groups by host and exact component/target/requester/CLSID context, preserving all PIDs, record IDs, and hashes. PID is not in the grouping key because a repeatedly launched requester can receive a new PID; process path remains in the key. `where failure_events>=3` applies after aggregation. Three different targets or components never combine. No CIM search is supplied because Change/Application State semantics would erase the event-specific failure contract.

Route 10010 to the application/Windows owner for the server identifier; route 10028 to the requesting application owner and target/network owners. Page only when the owned application is critical, a transaction/service is failing, multiple sources lose one target, or frequency exceeds the approved severity policy. Otherwise create a ticket/investigation. Recovery is not the absence of another event alone: require source health plus successful application transaction/service/component activation, target/RPC reachability for 10028, and an owner-defined quiet period.

## Step 3 — Validate detection, collection, and operational safety

Create schema-valid XML fixtures from redacted local exports. Test each event branch; exactly 2/3/4 events; mixed event IDs; multiple hosts/components/targets/requesters/CLSIDs; same requester with changing PID; absent/empty `param1`-`param4`; provider/channel collision; 10016 flood; duplicate record; localized Message with stable XML names; unknown event version; newest-window exclusion; delayed arrival; and earliest/latest boundaries. Assert exact output columns, grouping, counts, hashes, and fail-closed behavior. Test field-health alerts separately.

In a nonproduction application, use owner-approved safe actions. For 10010, prefer replaying a captured fixture unless the vendor supplies a reversible method to delay/fail server registration; do not corrupt registration or kill shared RPCSS. For 10028, use an isolated lab target and approved network/service interruption with an explicit rollback; do not alter production firewall or remote activation rights for testing. Confirm raw Event Viewer XML, indexed event, base result, routing, alert/ticket, owner acknowledgement, restoration, successful transaction, and quiet-period closure.

Exercise normal reboot/sign-in, patch/application upgrade, remote maintenance, decommissioned target, application fallback, slow startup, and duplicate collection. Verify an exception can suppress notification only for its exact tuple/time while worsening or unrelated failures still surface. Measure event rate/cardinality, bytes, lag, missing-field rate, search runtime, alert latency, owner response, and recovery duration. Record Windows/forwarder/TA/Splunk versions, fixture/export hash, search SID, dispatch/alert/case IDs, exact UTC bounds, expected/actual rows, and approvals. Keep status `draft` until Windows, application, network, and Splunk owners sign the tested contract.

## Step 4 — Triage and response

For Event 10010: (1) verify raw provider/channel/template and repeated count; (2) resolve the exact server identifier through approved inventory and read-only registration/application package evidence; (3) correlate service/process start, Application/System errors, Windows Error Reporting, hangs/crashes, CPU/disk/profile pressure, dependency state, reboot/sign-in, and patch/change; (4) run the affected application's supported health check or transaction; and (5) engage its owner/vendor. Do not assume the identifier is an AppID, a broken DLL, or a permission failure.

For Event 10028: (1) verify source host, target, requester path/PIDs, optional CLSID, and raw message; (2) confirm target is expected and still in inventory; (3) test name resolution and target availability from the correct source/security context; (4) inspect endpoint-mapper and dynamic-RPC reachability, firewall/network drops, RPCSS/target service state, and authentication/GPO changes using approved tools; (5) correlate whether other source hosts or applications fail to the same target; and (6) validate the requester transaction. Microsoft RPC guidance explains endpoint mapper TCP 135 followed by a dynamically assigned endpoint; opening only 135 is not proof that the complete path works, and broad firewall changes are not an automatic remedy.

Escalate when a critical transaction/service is impaired, one target fails from many sources, failures persist beyond reboot/maintenance, the target is unexpectedly absent, the requester crashes/hangs, source-health is good and frequency accelerates, or no owner exists for an active dependency. Preserve event and configuration evidence before change.

Never automatically modify HKCR/HKLM COM registration, run arbitrary `regsvr32`, change DCOM launch/access permissions, reset default security, widen RPC dynamic ports, disable firewall, restart RPCSS, uninstall packages, kill shared processes, or reboot. Those changes are component- and environment-specific, can weaken security or disrupt unrelated services, and Microsoft explicitly warns against permission edits merely to silence common 10016 events. Follow vendor/Microsoft-supported, owner-approved remediation and rollback. Validate application function and DCOM/RPC path after repair.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot

- **No events:** prove System-channel freshness, expected host scope, event occurrence, input/forwarder/deployment, `btool`, XML rendering, TA parsing, index/source/sourcetype, role access, and time bounds. Do not lower the threshold to compensate for missing data.
- **Provider is `DCOM` rather than full name:** inspect XML and extraction precedence; normalize only after a build-specific fixture proves equivalence. The production search intentionally requires the full Microsoft provider.
- **`param` fields missing:** inspect raw XML and event Version/local template. Update the versioned mapping/test before SPL; never parse localized Message as the primary contract.
- **10028 lacks `param4`:** supported variants may not render a CLSID. Preserve `not_provided`, group by target/requester, and do not fabricate one.
- **10010 identifier cannot be resolved:** use application inventory, package/service/task context and read-only registry evidence; assign ownership. Do not register/delete a class speculatively.
- **Many 10016 events but no result:** expected—the UC deliberately excludes them according to Microsoft guidance. Investigate only a separately scoped, impact-backed requirement.
- **Threshold unexpectedly high:** check duplicate inputs/forwarders and EventRecordID/hash duplication before tuning. Avoid silent deduplication that hides collection defects.
- **10028 while target responds:** DCOM/RPC activation can still fail while ping or another protocol works; validate endpoint mapper, returned dynamic endpoint, requester context, target service and actual transaction.
- **Alert after maintenance:** verify event time versus index time, delayed collection, exact exception bounds, target/component tuple, and later recovery. Do not extend a wildcard maintenance suppression.
- **No repeat events but app remains broken:** DCOM events are symptoms, not continuous health. Application/service transaction monitoring must own persistent failure and recovery.
grandmaExplanation: Some Windows programs ask shared components to start locally or on another computer. If the same component repeatedly starts too slowly, or one program repeatedly cannot reach the other computer, we show the support team exactly which program or destination needs checking.
